body.text: Labor's migration plan is based on what it can control: filling out the paperwork
Australia's migration policy is often described with cliched words like thorny, fractious, charged or vexed. But another word might do a better job: weird.

It was weird when the first federal parliament in 1901 screened out migrants from some countries with a dictation test set not in English, but in a European language chosen at random (including Scottish Gaelic).

Decades earlier, it was South Australia's weird idea to entice migrants through a sort of pyramid scheme. Land was sold to locals, the proceeds subsidised the voyages of newcomers, the newcomers bought more land, and so on.

More recently, there was the law to deter boat arrivals by stipulating that Australia was not actually Australian territory, at least not for migration purposes. Or the visa to attract migrants to "the regions", with a list of regions that included Melbourne.
This week's entry into the annals of weirdness came from Tony Burke, who said he was "really pleased" to be abandoning a cap on backpackers he had announced weeks ago.
Instead of capping that program, or any program, Burke assured the public that his migration target could be met by processing migrant applications really, really slowly.

The aims have been varied, but whether governments have wanted more migrants or fewer, or to sort the "right" kind from the "wrong" kind, the common thread has been their roundabout ways of pursuing an outcome.

There's a reason. Politicians talk about migration like something they control, with taps they can turn on and off at will, and visa streams they can easily redirect. But behind the stats and figures are unpredictable humans, who often thwart their intentions.
As Burke has learned, the weirdness is often a last resort, because "deciding who comes here" is harder than it sounds.
Who comes here
Consider Labor's current predicament, which is… thorny, fractious, charged and vexed.

Having conceded to One Nation and the Coalition that migration is too high, it is locked in a reverse bidding war to cut the intake to some lower figure. As the party in charge, it is the only party that can be held accountable for its target.

Ideally, a target would be chosen in a principled way. Decide how many international students there should rightly be, how many backpackers, how many family visas, skilled workers and refugees, add them all up and you have your target.

Burke, a self-styled political fixer, did the opposite. He started with Treasury's forecast for net migration, of 245,000 this year and 225,000 next year, and reverse-engineered a policy to get there.

A forecast is an unusual choice for a target. It is a prediction of what will happen, not a prescription for what should. And net migration is only loosely related to the number of migrants in the country, since it tracks the comings and goings of locals and foreigners.

One Nation and the Coalition belatedly realised this, and have both moved away from net migration targets, instead establishing how much they want to slash the number of temporary visas by, exactly which streams they want to cut, and by how much.

That is an easier task from opposition or the crossbench, especially for One Nation, which has a narrower political base and seems more comfortable alienating large swathes of the public, as it did this week when it proposed to end all parent visas.

Labor cannot be so flippant. But with great responsibility comes great power. If Burke had outlined a vision for the right composition of the migration program, he could have baked it in by the time of the next election, fought on Labor's remade turf.
Instead, by adopting an arbitrary target, he relinquished the exercise of judgement.
This probably seemed like the easy option. Instead of picking a fight in any given area, modest cutbacks would be made across every program.

Plan A, as best as we can tell, would have capped students and backpackers, limited post-graduation visas and family reunions, and reduced the humanitarian intake. Some of these were announced, others never were. But not one of them has survived, with the backpackers the last domino to fall this week.

Instead, Burke has been left with the one thing he can control: the paperwork. A series of ministerial directives have sent almost all offshore visa applicants to the bottom of the pile, in the hope this will slow down their arrival enough to lower net migration.

It's not so much a policy solution as a stopgap to make up for the absence of one. At some point, this government or another government will have to revisit the various programs when the bottom of the pile becomes the whole pile.
The circumstances by which they come

Burke is not the first minister to reach for weirdness as a last resort. The examples mentioned above are just some of the peculiar twists in Australia's migration history, laid out in Mark Cully's book Waves of Plenty, published earlier this year.
Cully, a former chief economist at the Department of Immigration, tells of plenty of ministers and prime ministers whose best-laid plans for the migration system have come unstuck.

Quite often, when the layers of weirdness or incompetence are stripped back, the reason for the unpredictability is some larger shift in the economy and demography of the world, to which migration is just a backdrop.

After World War II, Labor's immigration minister, Arthur Calwell, hoped his expansion of the migration program would mostly attract British arrivals, but instead a large exodus from continental Europe remade the country.

The end of the White Australia policy, in Cully's telling, was less the result of a positive decision and more an inevitable by-product of Australia's growing economic ties in Asia. And it took an unexpected wave of Vietnamese refugees for its effects to really be seen.

In the 1980s and 1990s, the Hawke, Keating and Howard governments unleashed vast new streams of migration almost by accident, in the pursuit of new economic opportunities for Australia in a globalised world.
Many of those accidents shape the debates of today.

One was the decision in the 1980s to uncap university places for foreign students. Cully writes that Labor's education minister at the time, Susan Ryan, "didn't think there would be much demand … because the fees would be much too high. She plainly didn't understand market forces".

Another was the tilt towards skilled migration within the permanent program, framed as an economic benefit since skilled workers found higher-paying jobs and paid more tax, but coming at the expense of larger family reunion backlogs, still a feature today.

Yet another was the expansion of temporary skilled visas, conceived as a way to plug specific gaps but eventually expanding to a vast class of "permanently temporary" workers, whose limbo status was the focus of the most recent migration review in 2023.

Cully observes that in 2006, treasurer Peter Costello "brusquely" declared that: "Australia has never been a guest worker country. We've never been a country where we bring you in and ship you out." At the time, half a million such workers were already here.

All three programs — international students, family reunions and temporary workers — are now in One Nation's sights. Its answer to the unexpected growth in each program is that they were a mistake and should be drastically curtailed.

Neither Labor nor the Coalition will go that far, weighing any cuts to the programs against workplace gaps in the care and construction sectors, and the importance of the family reunion program to the many Australians with close ties overseas.

These are hard decisions. Cully's closing remarks could be comforting, disconcerting or both for those in charge of making them: "Every attempt to imagine the future gets it wrong, usually badly. The future can't be seen; the curves always catch us by surprise."
At a time of high inflation, climbing unemployment, a stagnant economy, speculation about a recession and an unstable world, sensible policymaking is more important and yet all the more difficult.
